questions.q: What is the energy of a photon of light of wavelength 500 nm? (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\))

questions.solution: One electronvolt is the energy gained by an electron moved through 1 V, which is \(1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\). So \(2.0 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.2 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\). To go from eV to joules, multiply by \(e\).

questions.q: A metal has a work function of \(3.3 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\). What is its threshold frequency? (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\))
questions.solution: At the threshold frequency a photon has just enough energy to free an electron: \(hf_{0} = \phi\). So \(f_{0} = \frac{\phi}{h} = \frac{3.3 \times 10^{-19}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} = 5.0 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}\).

questions.q: Photons of energy \(6.0 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\) fall on a metal of work function \(3.5 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\). What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
questions.solution: \(hf = \phi + E_{k(max)}\), so \(E_{k(max)} = 6.0 \times 10^{-19} - 3.5 \times 10^{-19} = 2.5 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\). The work function is the energy used to escape; what is left is kinetic energy.

questions.q: Light above the threshold frequency falls on a metal surface. The intensity of the light is doubled, with the frequency unchanged. What happens to the photoelectrons?

options.A: Twice as many are emitted each second, with the same maximum kinetic energy.
options.B: The same number are emitted each second, with twice the maximum kinetic energy.
options.C: Twice as many are emitted each second, with twice the maximum kinetic energy.

questions.solution: Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons arriving each second, and each photon frees at most one electron. The energy of each photon, \(hf\), is unchanged, so the maximum kinetic energy stays the same.

questions.q: Which observation of the photoelectric effect cannot be explained by the wave model of light?

options.A: Electrons are emitted from a metal surface.
options.B: Brighter light releases more electrons each second.
options.C: Energy is transferred from the light to the electrons.
options.D: Below a threshold frequency no electrons are emitted, however bright the light.

questions.solution: A wave would deliver energy continuously, so light of any frequency should free electrons if it is bright enough or shines for long enough. The threshold frequency shows that light arrives as photons, each of energy \(hf\), absorbed one electron at a time.

questions.q: Photoelectrons leave a metal surface with a maximum kinetic energy of \(2.4 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\). What is the stopping potential? (\(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
questions.solution: The stopping potential is the potential difference that just stops the fastest electrons: \(eV_{s} = E_{k(max)}\). So \(V_{s} = \frac{2.4 \times 10^{-19}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}}\) = 1.5 V.

questions.q: What happens when an atom is ionised?

options.A: An electron moves to a higher energy level but stays in the atom.
options.B: An electron is removed from the atom completely.
options.C: An electron drops to a lower energy level and emits a photon.

questions.solution: Ionisation removes an electron from the atom altogether, leaving a positive ion. Moving an electron to a higher level without removing it is excitation. Both can be caused by a collision with a free electron or by absorbing a photon.

questions.q: An electron in an atom falls from an energy level at −1.5 eV to one at −3.4 eV. What is the wavelength of the photon emitted? (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
questions.solution: Photon energy is the difference between the levels: 3.4 − 1.5 = 1.9 eV, which is \(1.9 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.04 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\). Then \(\lambda = \frac{hc}{E} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}}{3.04 \times 10^{-19}} = 6.5 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\).

questions.q: The light from a hot gas forms a line spectrum. What does this show about the atoms of the gas?

options.A: Their electrons can only have certain discrete energies.
options.B: Their electrons can have any energy.
options.D: They are all moving at the same speed.

questions.solution: Each line is photons of one energy, emitted when an electron falls between two energy levels. Only certain photon energies appear, so the atom can only have certain discrete energy levels: \(hf = E_{1} - E_{2}\).

questions.q: What is the purpose of the coating on the inside of a fluorescent tube?

options.A: To stop electrons escaping from the tube.
options.C: To conduct the current along the tube.
options.D: To absorb ultraviolet photons and emit photons of visible light.

questions.solution: Excited mercury atoms in the tube emit ultraviolet photons. Atoms in the coating absorb these and are excited; they then de-excite in smaller steps, emitting photons of lower energy in the visible range.

questions.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at \(2.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)? (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(m_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}\))
questions.solution: \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.0 \times 10^{6}} = 3.6 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}\). This is about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why crystals diffract electrons.

questions.q: A beam of electrons passes through a thin crystal and forms a pattern of rings on a screen. What does this show?
questions.solution: The rings are a diffraction pattern, and diffraction is a wave property. So particles such as electrons also have a wave nature, with a wavelength given by \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\).

questions.q: In an electron diffraction experiment the electrons are made to travel faster. What happens to the diffraction rings?

options.A: They get larger, because the wavelength increases.
options.B: They get larger, because the wavelength decreases.
options.D: They get smaller, because the wavelength decreases.

questions.solution: Faster electrons have more momentum, and \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\), so their wavelength is shorter. A shorter wavelength is diffracted through smaller angles, so the rings move closer together.

questions.q: Which pair gives evidence for the particle nature of light and for the wave nature of electrons, in that order?

options.A: Diffraction of light; the photoelectric effect

questions.solution: The photoelectric effect shows light delivering energy in separate photons: its particle nature. Electron diffraction shows particles spreading and interfering like waves. Together they are the evidence for wave–particle duality.

questions.q: The graph shows the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons from a metal against the frequency of the light. What does the intercept on the frequency axis represent?

figure.alt: Maximum kinetic energy against frequency: a straight line that starts on the frequency axis at 5.0 times ten to the fourteen hertz and rises steadily.

options.A: The threshold frequency of the metal.
options.B: The work function of the metal.

questions.solution: \(E_{k(max)} = hf - \phi\). The line meets the frequency axis where the maximum kinetic energy is zero, so \(hf_{0} = \phi\): this is the threshold frequency, below which no electrons are emitted. The gradient of the line is the Planck constant, and the work function is the size of the intercept the line would make on the energy axis.
